title: Al-Tusi's observatory
hook: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi builds an observatory at Maragha under Mongol rule

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mongols become Muslim, and Ghazan takes the name Mahmud. Your line was: the conquerors converted. Did you give someone a fresh chance? Day nine hundred sixty-two.

On a hilltop above the town of Maragha, in Persia, workmen are laying stone for a building whose whole purpose is to watch the sky. Inside will go great instruments for measuring where the stars and planets stand, and a library to go with them. The money comes from Hulagu, the same Mongol prince whose army sacked Baghdad. And the man in charge is a Persian scholar, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. The storm that, the chroniclers say, drowned books in a river is now paying for star charts. Today's words: al-Tusi's observatory.
screen: `A HILLTOP ABOVE MARAGHA.` → `INSTRUMENTS AND A LIBRARY.` → `PAID FOR BY HULAGU.`

segments.voice: Al-Tusi was a scholar of many fields: astronomy, mathematics, philosophy, ethics, and the theology of the Shia tradition he belonged to. He came into Hulagu's service, and he persuaded the prince to build the observatory at Maragha. Scholars came to work there. They watched the sky night after night, measured, and wrote down tables of where the heavens moved, tables that astronomers went on using. And al-Tusi worked on a hard problem from the old Greek astronomy he had inherited: how to explain the planets' motions using only circles turning evenly. His answer is now called the Tusi couple. Picture a small circle rolling around inside a bigger one, twice as wide. A point on the small circle doesn't go round and round. It goes straight back and forth, in a line. Two circles, making a straight line. Some historians have noticed a very similar device in Copernicus's work, much later, and they still debate how it got there. So the line for today: learning survived. Not untouched. Not without a cost. But the habit of looking up and measuring carefully didn't die with Baghdad. It moved to a hilltop and kept going. Why would a believer care about tables of the stars? Partly for prayer: the times of prayer and the direction of Mecca are worked out from the sky. And partly because the Qur'an keeps pointing up. In surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! In the creation of the heavens and the earth and (in) the difference of night and day are tokens (of His sovereignty) for men of understanding." For al-Tusi's circle, measuring the sky was one way of reading those tokens.
screen: `A SCHOLAR OF MANY FIELDS.` · `TABLES OF THE MOVING HEAVENS.` · `THE TUSI COUPLE: CIRCLES MAKE A LINE.` · `TOKENS FOR MEN OF UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `LEARNING SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the stars. If it's dark where you are, step outside or go to a window and look up. If it's daytime, look at the sky as it is, or close your eyes and remember the last night sky you really saw. Don't name anything. Just look. Notice how much is up there that you didn't put there, that keeps its own time without you. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can bring to mind the words the Qur'an gives just after that verse: our Lord, you did not create this in vain. If you don't, simply let the size of it sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Al-Tusi's observatory. Built at Maragha under Mongol rule by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, a place to measure the sky after the fall of Baghdad. Today's words.
Your line: learning survived. Tonight, look up once before bed, and learn the name of one thing you see there: a star, a planet, the phase of the moon. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims use the sky to set the times of prayer, the direction of Mecca and the months of the lunar calendar, and the sighting of the new moon marks the start and end of Ramadan for communities that follow local sighting.
